findings.disposition: exempted — non-blocking: the panels are individually legible and the shape identity makes the zoom inferable; recording it so a later caption or panel-title edit can act on it
findings.summary: The scene carries two panels of the same plasma at two extents and neither panel is named: the left panel draws the whole machine with the CS stack and PF coils, the right one is a tight zoom on the wall region drawn over the same cell mesh. Nothing in the raster and nothing in the evidence fragment's caption (alt text: 'ITER poloidal mesh with labelled coil sections and the first wall') says which panel is which, and the script builds both from the same geometry without a title (scripts/prototypes/iter_bank/render.py:303 loops over the overview and detail bounds). A reader must infer that the right panel is the same mesh enlarged rather than a second or different machine state; naming each panel, or saying in the caption that the right panel is the wall detail, removes the inference.

findings.disposition: exempted — non-blocking: the wall renders with a visible dash pattern (190 separated segments measured in the raster) and the legend matches the drawn mark, so a reader can map the entry to the curve
findings.summary: The first wall's only separation from the coil mark is a fine dash between two closely related greys: #9aa2ab over coil #929292, dashed 5.0 pt on and 2.5 pt off at linewidth 1.7 (render.py:25-26). In the delivered 1400-pixel raster the wall segments into about 190 dash components of 20-43 pixels, so at a page column width of roughly 900 pixels a dash is 4-5 pixels and the wall reads as a near-continuous hairline where it hugs the plasma edge; the dash is only just perceptible. The mark is distinguishable and the legend carries the same dash, so this does not hold the node; a longer dash period or a stronger lightness step would make the first wall read as a separate component at page scale.
